list.listitem: Common symptoms of lichen sclerosus (LS) include pruritus, pain, and/or dyspareunia. C
Skin punch biopsy in the most sclerotic area of the lesion is usually diagnostic. Ulcerated or vegetative lesions should also be biopsied to rule out squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). C

Treatment options include an ultrapotent topical steroid (considered first-line), A topical calcineurin inhibitors (eg, tacrolimus or pimecrolimus; second line), B acitretin (contraindicated in pregnancy), B UV light treatment for extragenital lesions, C possibly focused ultrasound therapy or laser therapy (vulvar LS), B and surgery (circumcision) for penile LS and associated urethral stricture (urethroplasty). B
Relapse is common. B
Up to 10% of persons with vulvar LS may develop SCC in sclerotic areas over time. C

background.definition: LS is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the skin and mucosa characterized by hypocellular fibrosis (sclerosis), affecting all age groups and both men and women. LS is more common in women with a female-to-male ratio ranging from 10 to 1 to 6 to 1. Genital skin and mucosa are affected most often, but extragenital LS also occurs over other skin areas such as the back and shoulders. LS is sometimes called lichen sclerosus et atrophicus or von Zambusch's disease.

list.listitem: In an electronic medical records study of men in the Armed Forces, the incidence of male LS was 1.4 patients per 100,000 visits; the incidence was higher among white patients (2.1/100,000 visits), especially after the age of 60 years.
In one general gynecology practice, over a 3-year period, 28 women (1.7%) had biopsy-proven LS.
The prevalence of vulvar LS in a pediatric vulvar clinic in the United Kingdom was 1 in 900, similar to the US figure of 1 in 1,000.
Other reviews list a prevalence among adult women of 1 in 1000.
In a case series of 202 patients with LS, most (79%) were 50 years or older. Mean age at onset for women in another study was 55.1 years and for girls 5.4 years.
SCC can develop within LS (see Prognosis section).
LS accounts for up to 10% of urethral stricture disease in men; in a database study of 1,151 men with LS, 81 (7.0%) had LS-related urethral stricture.

Sexual dysfunction is more common in patients with LS. In a case-control study, women with LS reported less frequent sexual activity, less vaginal intercourse, and less satisfaction with sexual activity than healthy controls and Candida controls. In a survey study of 771 men with LS, more than half reported that LS had a negative influence on their sexual health. In this study, 1% reported penile SCC.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 23 studies including 486 subjects with LS found a prevalence of sexual dysfunction of 59% (95% CI 48 - 70%); dyspareunia was the most reported type of dysfunction.
Unknown.
Likely genetic predisposition; keratinocytes of LS express tumor suppressor gene p53 protein.
The bimodal presentation in young children and postmenopausal women and the higher incidence in individuals with Turner syndrome suggest that a low estrogen state may be a contributing factor.
Lichen sclerosus has been reported after therapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Theories regarding causes of LS include infection, autoimmune factors and chronic irritation (eg, friction, genital piercing, surgery).

Infection: there is evidence of infection with Borrelia burgdorferi, a bacteria of the spirochete class (also the agent of Lyme disease). There is also an association with human papilloma virus (HPV). Authors of a systematic review of 27 papers found a median prevalence of HPV of 22% (range 0% to 80%) of LS cases with a higher prevalence among males than females (29% and 8%, respectively). HPV16 was the most prevalent genotype although low-risk genotypes were also reported.
Autoimmune factors: in one case series, 20% had elevated thyroid antibodies and 17% had a history of psoriasis. Autoantibody to glycoprotein extracellular matrix protein 1 has been implicated.
Histopathology: disease features may include basal cell degeneration, upper dermal edema, homogenization of collagen, and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate.

In a study of 83 men undergoing urethroplasty for stricture, the 58 patients with LS had more associated inflammation. Some inflammatory markers, and all cases positive for viral staining (although rare), were only identified among LS cases.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Areas of skin trauma or surgery
Presence of morphea, especially plaque morphea

list.listitem: Compliance with individualized preventive topical corticosteroid treatment that achieves normal skin color and texture may reduce risk of adhesions, scarring, and vulvar neoplasms. B

In a prospective longitudinal cohort study of 507 women with biopsy-proven vulvar LS, women who were adherent to topical corticosteroid regimens (70.4%) were less likely than women who were only partially adherent to have adhesions and scarring (3.4% vs. 40%) and vulvar SCC or vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (0% vs. 4.7%); they were also more likely to have symptom suppression (93.3% vs. 58%). Rates of cutaneous atrophy were similar (1.1% vs. 2%, respectively).
Common symptoms include pruritus, pain, and/or dyspareunia. C
Skin punch biopsy in the most sclerotic area of the lesion is usually diagnostic. Ulcerated or vegetative lesions should also be biopsied to rule out SCC. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pruritic, trigger identified (eg, perfumed soaps, clothing dye), skin lichenification but no scarring
Chalk-white macules, asymptomatic, other skin areas affected (eg, periorificial, trunk), often symmetrically
Patient describes itch-scratch-itch cycle, may have underlying dermatitis or infection
Silver-white scale on erythematous plaques; common on scalp, elbows, but rarely on genitals
Purplish pruritic papules on skin associated with oral and vulvar white striae that are usually asymptomatic
Erythematous plaques becoming sclerotic with central clearing and erythematous borders
Ulcerated lesion with indurated border within sclerotic lesion; failure to heal

list.listitem: Common symptoms include pruritus, pain, and/or dyspareunia. Based on a retrospective chart review of 81 consecutive patients with biopsy-proven LS, 98% had pruritus and 61% reported irritation with burning and dyspareunia.
In a survey study of 771 men with LS, pruritus, tenderness and pain were frequently reported and phimosis (narrowing of the foreskin opening preventing retraction) was common.

Other symptoms in children include purpura, dysuria, constipation, pain with defecation and genital erosions. For boys, phimosis and inability to retract the foreskin are presenting concerns. Other symptoms in males include dysuria, decreased sensation in the glans, and urethral discharge.
Bleeding can occur from trauma due to scratching.
In a study in general gynecology practice, about one-third of the patients were asymptomatic; of these 11 women, 7 had scarring of the clitoral prepuce or resorption of the labia minora.

The early appearance of vulvar LS consists of white, polygonal papules that coalesce into smooth white plaques with size varying from a few millimeters to obliteration of the labia minora with stenosis of the introitus. An hourglass appearance may be seen with perivaginal and perianal LS, with minimal involvement of the perineum in between. In the case series above, most patients (76%) had labial involvement, 70% had clitoral involvement, 68% had perineal lesions, and 32% had perianal LS.

LS can occur on oral mucosa. Authors of a systematic review found 41 reported cases of histologically-confirmed LS; the mean age was 31 years and 66% were women. Oral LS was usually asymptomatic and located on the labial mucosa in 20 cases, lip in 15, buccal mucosa in 14, gingiva in 12, tongue in 12, and palate in 7 cases. No cases of cancer were reported.
Inflammation can result in separation of sections of the epidermis resulting in blisters and bullae.
Skin punch biopsy in the most sclerotic area of the lesion is recommended and is usually diagnostic. Ulcerated or vegetative lesions should also be biopsied to rule out SCC.

The American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ACOG) recommends vulvar biopsy for lesions that are atypical (eg, new pigmentation, indurated, affixed to underlying tissue, bleeding, or ulcerated), when there is concern for malignancy, lesions in a patient who is immunocompromised, if the diagnosis is uncertain, lesions that do not respond to standard therapy or if the disease worsens during therapy (consensus recommendation).
Toluidine blue staining can be used to direct biopsy; it has higher uptake in patients with vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), although 10% of women with LS also demonstrate staining.
A punch biopsy should be considered for diagnosis in a patient with persistent vulvar papules or plaques; biopsy should be performed on areas of ulceration or vegetative lesions to rule out SCC.

According to the 2018 Japanese guidelines, LS should be biopsy proven; the conditions to exclude are localized scleroderma, chronic eczema, vitiligo vulgaris and lichen planus. The guidelines also suggest a severity classification with 1 point given for multiple lesions or spreading skin lesions and 2 points for lesion-related functional disorder; 2 or more points indicate severe disease.

Girls with LS are often suspected of being victims of sexual abuse due to the erosions, fissures, hematomas, bleeding, and scarring that are often present. While it is reasonable to ask about abuse given that the two conditions can occur together, proper diagnosis can prevent additional emotional trauma to patients and families.

An ultrapotent topical steroid (eg, 0.05% clobetasol propionate ointment) appears effective for symptom improvement in most patients but is less effective for physical signs. A Efficacy has been reported in approximately 60% to 80% of cases. Co-treatment with emollients is recommended for genital LS. C

Alternative treatments include petrolatum ointment, C topical calcineurin inhibitors (eg, 0.1% tacrolimus or 1% pimecrolimus cream twice daily), B and acitretin (20-30 mg/d); B the latter is contraindicated in pregnancy.
Focused ultrasound therapy and laser therapy were found to be effective in single trials. B

ACOG recommends use of a medium-potency or high-potency topical corticosteroid ointment for initial treatment of LS. The EuroGuiderm 2024 guideline recommends either ultrapotent or potent topical corticosteroids in females and males, adults and children as the gold standard for genital LS with co-treatment with emollients.
The use of an ultrapotent topical steroid such as 0.05% clobetasol propionate ointment is effective for symptom improvement, but is less effective for physical signs.

In one case series, 66% were symptoms free following treatment, but only 22% had complete resolution. Authors of another case series, using clobetasol, found complete remission occurred in 54% but there was a high relapse rate (84% at 4 years).

A systematic review of 17 studies of conservative treatments for penile and urethral lichen sclerosus concluded that topical corticosteroids are the mainstay of conservative treatment. For eample, 0.05% clobetasol cream twice daily for 7 weeks for penile LS after prior surgery found that 9/21 (43%) were clinically free of LS on exam and 100% reported reduced symptoms at an average of 14.6-months follow-up. Tacrolimus is recommended as alternative or adjunctive therapy as needed.

In a randomized clinical trial (RCT) of 64 women with vulvar LS, tapered vs. continuous administration of mometasone furoate 0·1% ointment was equally effective (84% vs. 78% were considered responders, respectively) and well tolerated.
ACOG recommends consideration of intralesional corticosteroids for LS that is poorly controlled or resistant to topical corticosteroids.

Twice daily intraurethral clobetasol cream was successful in preventing need for urethroplasty in 40 men with LS-associated urethral stricture. Authors of the systematic review cited above also found use of 0.05% clobetasol cream twice daily 4-8 weeks for urethral LS after surgery successful in most patients, with 36/42 (85.7%) not requiring subsequent surgical management at an average of 8-months follow-up.

British Academy of Dermatology guidelines recommend as second line therapy intralesional triamcinolone 10 to 20 mg in men and women with LS who are not responsive to topical steroids (assuming malignancy has been ruled out).

These are second-line options. ACOG recommends consideration of topical calcineurin inhibitors for patients with a confirmed diagnosis of LS that does not respond to topical or intralesional corticosteroids or for patients at risk of skin atrophy.

One percent pimecrolimus cream twice daily was found effective for symptom relief in several small case series of women with vulvar LS. In one RCT, pimecrolimus was as effective as clobetasol in symptom relief and investigator global ratings but less effective in improving inflammation. There is a case report of the rapid appearance of a vulvar SCC in a 73-year-old woman following initiation of this treatment.

Authors of a Cochrane review of topical agents confirmed effectiveness for clobetasol propionate, mometasone furoate, and pimecrolimus in treating genital LS. Based on one trial reviewed, there was no difference between pimecrolimus and clobetasol propionate in symptom relief but the former was less effective with respect to investigator-rated global improvement. These authors also found no benefit from testosterone cream, dihydrotestosterone, and progesterone; in fact, testosterone cream worsened symptoms when used as maintenance therapy after steroid treatment.

Post circumcision for penile LS, authors of a systematic review found 18/20 (80%) had a complete response without relapse at 13-months follow-up with topical 0.1% tacrolimus. For urethral LS, these authors found 1g 0.03% tacrolimus instillation twice daily for 6 weeks then once nightly for 3 months resulted in significantly improved postvoid residual and flow rate at 3 months in 75% (15/20).
The 2018 Japanese guidelines note that while tacrolimus ointment is a treatment option, it is less effective than topical corticosteroids.

In a case series of men with penile LS, monthly anesthetic/steroid subdermal injection in conjunction with high-potency steroids resulted in more rapid resolution of pruritus in those with moderate (6 vs. 19 weeks) and severe (9 vs. 24 weeks) LS, although patients were less satisfied with injections.

In a small case series of patients with refractory extragenital LS, a combination of pulsed high-dose corticosteroids combined with low-dose methotrexate resulted in a significant decrease in clinical score with no relapses within 3 months.
In one small RCT, acitretin (20-30 mg/d for 16 weeks) was more effective (14 of 22 patients improved) than placebo.

In a 20-week RCT of 49 patients with severe genital LS, a complete response was achieved by 36% randomized to acitretin vs. 6% of controls; 36% achieved partial response compared to 12.5% of controls, respectively. Mean total clinical score of the acitretin group was significantly lower at week and significantly greater improvement in DLQI quality of life scores was reported.

In an RCT including 37 premenopausal women with histologically proven vulvar LS, standard treatment with topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% was superior to treatment with topical progesterone 8% ointment; LS was in complete remission in 13/16 patients on standard treatment vs. 6/10 in the progesterone arm.

Other drugs under evaluation include intralesional adalimumab and intradermal loco-regional polydeoxyribonucleotides for men. Adalimumab (a TNF-alpha blocking monoclonal antibody) was reported to be effective in a case report with 2 patients.

In an RCT of 29 patients with biopsy-proven LS, there were no significant differences in lesion inflammation between those randomized to 2 separate treatments of autologous PRP injections vs. placebo saline injections.

In another RCT including 20 patients with vulvar LS nonresponsive to topical steroids randomized to two nanofat–PRP injections 3 months apart or continued topical 0.05% clobetasol propionate cream (controls), patients in the intervention arm had significant improvement in symptoms and signs (eg, erosions) at 12-month follow-up compared to baseline and better quality-of-life scores from baseline which were significantly higher than the control group.

In a case series of 215 patients with LS of the foreskin and/or anterior urethra undergoing surgical treatment including circumcision, meatotomy or urethroplasty, no postoperative instrumentation was required at an average follow-up of 56 months; success rates ranged from 72% to 100%.

Authors of another case series of 31 men following treatment of LS of the glans penis with resurfacing using skin grafting reported that 84% were fully satisfied with cosmetic and functional results, and 71% of them had resumed sexual activity at one year.

In a case series of 36 men with urethral stricture associated with LS, 1-stage urethroplasty with single or combined lingual or buccal mucosal grafts was successful in 88.9%. Urinary fistula occurred in 1 patient and meatal stenosis developed in 3 patients during a mean follow-up of 38.7 months.

In a systematic review of 21 papers of single-stage buccal mucosa urethroplasty for 625 patients with urethral strictures from LS, stricture recurrence was 10% (95% CI, 6-14%), with longer-term studies of ≥24-months reporting a recurrence rate of 18%. Use of penile invagination vs. penile skin incision was associated with lower recurrence.

Long-term follow-up of augmentation 1-stage urethroplasty, however, demonstrated a lower 5-year stricture-free survival rate of 0.77 (95% CI 0.71-0.83) based on a systematic review of 10 studies including 954 patients, some for LS. Fifteen-year stricture-free survival rate across all studies was only 0.45 (95% CI 0.35-0.57).

In a single institution case series of 733 patients undergoing urethroplasty with at least 100 months of follow-up, cumulative incidence of stricture recurrence was 6%, 10%, and 12% after 1, 5, and 10 years, respectively. Most (89%) of patients reported being satisfied with the outcome of surgery. However, a diagnosis of LS (hazard ratio [HR] 4.5, 95% CI 2.3-9.5) as well as stricture length (HR 1.1), prior radiation (HR 4.2), and infectious etiology (HR 5.3) increased recurrence rates.

In a case series of 79 men with LS-associated urethral stricture managed by three different surgeries—single-stage buccal mucosa graft (BMG) urethroplasty, 2-stage BMG urethroplasty, or perineal urethrostomy—the latter was considered most successful at 93%.

In a case series of 23 women undergoing posterior vestibuloplasty for LS-associated disabling sexual dysfunction (5 women also undergoing anterior vestibuloplasty with a free full-thickness graft of vaginal mucosa), postoperative infection occurred in 1 woman and reactivation in another. Long-term complications included localized pain in 3 women and reoperation in one woman.
Psychosexual counseling had a significant impact on sexual functioning and quality of life over usual care in an RCT including 158 Danish women with newly diagnosed LS.
Petrolatum ointment was found to be as effective as topical testosterone for symptoms in men. In this study, 75% of patients improved.

In one small RCT of 42 women with LS under treatment with clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment and vitamin E moisturizer, women randomized to wearing underwear made of Dermasilk showed better improvement in clinical symptoms compared with women randomized to cotton briefs.
Focused ultrasound therapy was shown in one Chinese phase 2 trial to be very effective with an initial response rate of 94.7% and a 2-year disease free rate of 55% (17 of 31).

The American Urogynecologic Society 2022 consensus statement on vaginal energy-based devices was that laser therapy may be effective for LS. Two subsequent systematic reviews on use of laser for LS support its use for vulvar LS although authors note that most trials were underpowered, at risk for bias, and lacked long-term follow-up. No serious adverse events were reported.

In an RCT of 40 women with vulvar LS randomized to 3 laser treatments or topical steroids, women undergoing laser treatment had greater symptom improvement at 1, 3 and 6 months. Discomfort with laser was rated at 1.5 on a scale of 10.

In an RCT including 66 patients with vulvar LS, the 44 patients randomized to Nd:YAG/Er:YAG laser therapy had greater decreases in a validated clinical LS score than the 22 receiving topical clobetasol propionate therapy. However, there were no differences in improvement scores on a visual analogue scale for symptom severity or a vulvovaginal symptoms questionnaire, although patient satisfaction was higher with laser therapy.

Fractionated CO2 was not an effective monotherapy treatment for vulvar LS compared to sham laser treatment in an RCT including 37 patients based on histopathology scale score. Fractionated CO2 laser therapy was significantly better than steroid treatment in another RCT including 51 patients with vulvar LS based on change in Skindex-29 score at 6 months, patient report of symptom improvement (89% vs. 62%, respectively, rating symptoms as being "better or much better") and patient satisfaction.

Authors of a systematic review, despite limited data, concluded that full-spectrum UVA and UVA-1 phototherapy seemed effective in the treatment of sclerotic skin diseases, including LS. Short-term side effects of UVA-1 therapy were erythema, pruritus, xerosis cutis, tanning, and recrudescence of herpes simplex infection. Potential long-term risks of photoaging and skin cancer remain unknown.

In one case series, photodynamic therapy (6-courses every second week using 5-aminolevulinic acid as a photosensitizer followed by light exposure) had short-term success in about one-third of patients with LS.
ACOG recommends long-term, individualized topical corticosteroid therapy to maintain normality of skin color and texture and to prevent scarring in patients with LS.
Referral is suggested for patients with SCC and in cases resistant to recommended therapy.
Relapse is common; in one case series, relapse occurred in 84% at 4 years (95% CI, 57%-94%). B
Sexual difficulties may persist despite what appears to be adequate treatment. B
Most children with LS have persistence into adulthood although symptom improvement often occurs. C
In a cohort of symptomatic patients, 9% developed VIN and 21% invasive SCC; LS preceded SCC by 4 years (range 1-23 years).
In another cohort study, 9% developed vulvar SCC; these women had either been untreated or irregularly treated for their vulvar LS.

Authors of a systematic review of 15 studies of patients with anogenital LS found an absolute risk of SCC of between 0.21% and 3.9% for women and 0% to 0.91% for men across the included studies. The incidence rate was 0.65-8.89/1000 person-years for women and 0.00-6.49/1000 person-years for men.

In a case series of 223 men who underwent surgery for penile SCC, LS was present in 23% of patients but was not associated with increased rates of adverse histopathological features, including carcinoma in situ.
In a cohort study of 180 women with vulvar LS, 56% were asymptomatic at follow-up and 12% continued to have moderate to severe symptoms.

In a cohort study of 83 women with vulvar LS followed for a median of 4.7 years, complete remission was obtained in 54%; no women older than 70 years had remission. Relapse is common and estimated to occur in 84% at 4 years (95% CI, 57%-94%).

In one 12-week trial, despite 31 out of 36 enrolled women having adequate treatment of LS as determined by biopsy specimens, scores on the Female Sexual Distress Scale (although significantly decreased) remained at 15 or greater, indicating continued sexual distress.
Authors of a systematic review concluded that nearly 60% of women with LS suffered from sexual dysfunction to some degree.
ACOG recommends monitoring at 3 months following initial therapy for LS to assess response to therapy and ensure proper medication application.
Long-term follow-up is warranted as about 5% to 10% will develop SCC over time.
LS is a chronic disease that usually responds to treatment but is recurrent and, in about 5% to 10% of patients, results in vulvar cancer; continued follow-up is recommended.
None of the treatments have been proven safe in pregnancy (category C) and retinoids (eg, acitretin) are contraindicated in pregnancy (category X).

Authors of a systematic review identified 4516 cases of childhood LS including 2804 male, mean age of onset 8.6 years (range 2-15 years) and 1707 female patients, mean age of onset 6.5 years (range 4 months to 14 years). Most (99.6% and 94.6%, respectively) of the lesions were genital in both sexes. Symptoms were reported more frequently in girls than boys and included pruritus (49.6% vs. 0.1%), pain or burning sensations (28.2% vs. 0.9%), dysuria (15.9% vs. 6.9%) and constipation (14.9% vs. 0%). Clinical signs most frequently seen in girls were hypopigmentation and skin atrophy (59.6% and 45.4%, respectively) and scarring or genital anatomy changes (95.6%) most frequent in boys. Concomitant autoimmune disorders were rarely reported (1.5%). Remission by puberty occurred in about one quarter to one third of affected girls.
The diagnosis and treatment is similar for children and the disease does not necessarily remit after puberty.

The North American Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Gynecology (NASPAG) 2014 guidelines recommend diagnosis without biopsy in patients presenting with urogenital complaints including dysuria, dyschezia, and constipation and appearance of LS lesions, reserving biopsy for patients with atypical lesions or for those not responding to initial treatment. C
Removal of irritants such as lotions, soaps, frequent diaper changes and use of petrolatum is recommended.

There are no RCTs or long-term studies on children with LS. The NASPAG guidelines recommend high potency topical steroids as first-line treatment. B There is limited supporting evidence for use of immune modulators in non-responders or for those who do not tolerate steroids. B Topical calcineurin inhibitors are not approved for children under age 2 years.

In a case series of 14 girls with LS, aged 2 to 10 years, 13 had complete clearance and 1 partial clearance with topical clobetasol 0.05% ointment followed by tacrolimus 0.1% topical ointment for maintenance; clearance occurred over an average of 43.1 weeks (range 4-156 weeks).
Authors of a systematic review of 6 papers with 89 patients concluded that use of topical steroids for boys with LS-related phimosis avoided circumcision in 35%.

In one case series from England, preputioplasty, performed in 326 boys (4.1%) appears to be an alternative option to circumcision for LS, although subsequent circumcision was performed in 22%. Use of steroid injection reduced this risk (14% vs. 30% of those without steroid injection).
Antihistamines can be used for pruritus and persistent pain can be treated with tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline, desipramine), gabapentin, or serotonin reuptake inhibitors (fluoxetine).

Of 250 boys circumcised for LS (with pathologic confirmation), 55 had a meatal procedure at circumcision and 49 underwent subsequent meatal dilation or meatotomy for stricture. Interestingly, of the 50 boys who were circumcised for suspected LS but did not have LS histology, only 3 required a later meatal procedure.

NASPAG recommends that patients be followed at 6- to 12-month intervals to monitor for symptoms, architectural change, and possible risk of malignancy and for symptoms and signs of other autoimmune disorders. C
